02-060.r: Per capita annual income 1991-92 → about Rs. 7,500 (nearest option; Economic Survey 2022-23 gives Rs. 6835 at current prices).

02-061.r: Highest GDP growth in the 1990s → 1999-2000 (GNI growth 8.8%, 2011-12 series); 1996-97 had 7.7%.

02-062.r: Highest growth rate among the options → 2006-07 (as per 2011-12 series, Economic Survey 2022-23).

02-063.r: Five years to 2010-11: GDP and per capita income growth did not rise steadily (2008-09 dip: GNI 2.9%, PCI 0.8%) → neither statement correct.

02-065.r: Economic Survey 2020-21 (IMF estimate) → India's real GDP growth 11.5% in 2021-22 (financial year 2022) and 6.8% in 2022-23.

02-066.r: GDP growth 2005-06 at 1999-2000 prices → 8.4% (CSO revised estimate, 31 May 2006) = 8 to 9 per cent; later revised to 9.5%.

02-067.r: GDP growth 1998-99 → 6.5% (base year 1993-94); revised to 6.7% (base year 2004-05).

02-068.r: GDP growth up from 4.5% (2012-13) to 4.7% (2013-14) → high agriculture & allied growth (4.7% vs 1.4%) due to a favourable monsoon.

02-069.r: Economic Survey 2009-10 showed agriculture & allied with negative growth in 2009-10 over 2008-09; revised data show positive growth in every sub-sector.
02-069.c: Book gives no single answer: (a) agriculture fits the Economic Survey 2009-10, but revised data show no sub-sector with negative growth in 2009-10.

02-070.r: RBI's contemporary estimate of growth for 2002-03 → about 5-5.5%.

02-071.r: Asian Development Report 2004 (released 28 April 2004) → India's growth for 2005 estimated at 6.9%.

02-072.r: 1997-98: growth fell to 4.3% (from 8.0% in 1996-97) and public investment fell to 6.6% of GDP → A and R true, R not the explanation.

02-073.r: Growth rose (Sixth Plan 5.5%, Seventh 5.8%, Eighth 6.8%) as saving rate rose from 18.9% to 25.1% of GDP (1995-96) → A, R true; R explains A.

02-074.r: Per capita income 1998-99 (descending) → Punjab, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh (DABC); in 2021-22 Gujarat leads, then Maharashtra, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh.

02-075.r: Per capita NSDP (descending): question period → Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka (option d); 2021-22 → Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Maharashtra.
02-075.c: Book gives no single answer, but says (d) 3, 1, 4, 2 was right for the question period; by 2021-22 data the order is 2, 4, 1, 3, in no option.

02-076.r: Lowest per capita income (NSDP, 2021-22) → Bihar (Rs. 47498); highest → Goa (Rs. 472070).

02-079.r: Highest per capita income 2009-10 (data of March 2011) → Goa; lowest → Bihar (same in 2021-22).

02-080.r: Highest per capita NSDP 2021-22 among options → Karnataka (Rs. 265623), just above Haryana (Rs. 264835); Haryana led at question time.
02-080.t: Haryana is a very close second now and was first earlier; the book's current answer is Karnataka.

02-081.r: Highest GSDP growth in 2010-11 among options → Bihar; in 2021-22 Chhattisgarh (11.71%) led these, Manipur (13.51%) highest overall.

02-082.r: 1990s: effective growth till 1996-97 (not stagnant); foodgrains rose 176.4 → 212.9 million tonnes (1990-91 to 2001-02) → both A and R false.
02-082.c: Book gives no single answer: it finds both A and R false (growth was not stagnant and foodgrain output rose), and no option says that.

02-083.r: Book answer: A false (per capita income has improved along with national income since 1947); R true (sizeable population still below poverty line).
02-083.c: Printed answer (d) says A false, R true, but the explanation says A true, R false.

02-084.r: Rural incomes lower than urban → farmers lack scientific-agriculture knowledge, primary products priced below manufactured goods, low investment in agriculture (all three).

02-085.r: Capital formation → depends on savings and effective financial institutions; investment is its essential factor (both true).

02-086.r: Low growth despite high savings and capital formation → high capital-output ratio (capital needed for one unit of output).
02-086.h: High COR = more capital for the same output = slower growth.

02-087.r: High saving economy but output rises little → high capital-output ratio; lower COR means higher productivity of capital and faster growth.

02-088.r: Slow growth of per capita income in India → high capital-output ratio and high population growth (not capital formation or fiscal deficits).

02-089.r: Low per capita income in Uttar Pradesh → fast-growing population, lack of entrepreneurship, inadequate infrastructure; modernization of agriculture is not a cause.

02-090.r: Economic growth must occur with capital formation (saving part of income and investing it) → the most important factor of growth.

02-091.r: Most supportive for 8% or more growth in near future → implementing all stalled productive projects; GST, skills, ease of doing business help long-term.

02-092.r: Slow growth of real per capita income → rapid population growth, high price rise, slow agricultural and industrial growth; foreign exchange is now sufficient.

02-093.r: Highest gross domestic savings rate in 2001-2010 decade → 2007-08 (37.8% of GDP at current market prices).

02-094.r: Gross domestic savings rate then → 20-25% of GDP (23.9% in 1995-96; 22.8% in 1996-97).

02-095.r: Gross domestic savings rate 2012-13 → 33.9% of GDP, so none of the options.

02-096.r: Savings ratio 2006-07 → above 32% of GDP (34.9% at current market prices).

02-097.r: Largest contributor to savings in India → household sector (2001-02: 23.6% of GDP out of total 26.0%).

02-098.r: Question period → share of private corporate sector in savings increased (3.4% in 2001-02 to 10.2% in 2005-06).

02-099.r: Highest share in household savings → physical assets (more than deposits, currency, shares and debentures).

02-100.r: Share in savings (descending) → household sector > private corporate sector > public corporations/enterprises > government.

03-001.r: Nodal institution for coordination and implementation of SDGs (Agenda 2030) in India → NITI Aayog.

03-002.r: SDG Index 2016 → India 110th of 149 countries; SDG Index 2024 (SDSN) → 109th of 167 (score 63.99).

03-003.r: SDG Index 2017 → India 116th of 157 nations; 2023 → 112th of 166; 2024 → 109th of 167.

03-004.r: SDG India Index (NITI Aayog) 2019 and 2020-21 → Uttar Pradesh in 'Performer' category; Kerala topped both; Gujarat not in top five.

03-008.r: SDG India Index 2019 → Gujarat 'Performer' (64), not Front-Runner; 2020-21 → Gujarat Front-Runner (69); Kerala (75), Himachal, Tamil Nadu (74) front-runners.
03-008.c: Book gives no single answer: by the SDG India Index 2019, (c) Gujarat was a Performer, not a Front-Runner; by the 2020-21 index all four are Front-Runners.

03-009.r: SDG Urban Index 2021-22 (NITI Aayog, November 2021) → 1. Shimla, 2. Coimbatore, 3. Chandigarh and Thiruvananthapuram; Indore not in top ten.

03-010.r: SDG-6 → Clean Water and Sanitation: availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all by 2030 (17 SDGs).

03-011.r: SDG-10 → Reduced inequalities; SDG-13 → Climate Action; SDG-14 → Life below water; SDG-15 → Life on Land.

03-012.r: Annual SDG Progress Report → presented by UN Secretary General from global indicator framework and national statistical data (true); Global Sustainable Development Report → once every four years.

03-013.r: 'Limits to Growth' → Club of Rome (born April 1968 at a meeting in Rome); report published 1972.

03-014.r: Limits to Growth (Meadows, 1972) → limits reached in the next 100 years if trends continue unchanged; in 2004 Meadows cut it to 30 years.

03-015.r: Environmental Kuznets Curve → inverted 'U': environment worsens with early growth, then improves after a certain level of per capita GDP.

03-016.r: Term 'Sustainable Development' introduced in 1980 → IUCN's world conservation strategy.
03-016.t: Don't confuse 1980 (term introduced) with 1987 (Brundtland Report definition).

03-017.r: Sustainable development (Brundtland Report, 'Our Common Future') → meets present needs without compromising future generations' needs → A and R true, R explains A.

03-018.r: Saving energy and resources for the future without sacrificing present comfort → sustainable development (modern concept from 1987 Brundtland Report).

03-020.r: Balancing resource use with conserving resources for the future → sustainable development (WCED report 'Our Common Future', 1987).

03-021.r: Sustainable development is inherently linked with carrying capacity → maximum population an area can support sustainably.

03-022.r: Base of sustainable development → environmental approach (outlook).

03-023.r: Sustainable economic development → development of present generation that conserves natural resources for future generations (inter-generational use of natural resources).

03-025.r: Neemrana, a model of sustainable economic development → Alwar district, Rajasthan.

03-026.r: Sustainable tourism aim → manage tourism and environment while maintaining cultural integrity and ecological processes.

03-027.r: India-Norway Task Force on Blue Economy for Sustainable Development → launched January 2019.

03-028.r: Social capital → level of mutual trust and harmony in society (relationships, networks, shared norms); not literacy, buildings or working-age population.
